opus-5.5.text:
I'd describe my contribution as fairly indirect. Kimi Delta Attention was really the Kimi team's work. They did the hard part: deciding to bet on a hybrid linear architecture at scale, running the large experiments, and making it work in a production model.

What I can say is that it builds on a line of work I've been part of. Gated DeltaNet combined the delta rule with a gating, or decay, mechanism, but the decay there is coarse: one scalar per head. Kimi's move was to make the decay fine-grained, channel-wise, so different dimensions of the state can forget at different rates. That's a natural idea. It's similar in spirit to what GLA did for plain linear attention. But making it efficient with the delta rule is not trivial. Once each channel has its own decay, the chunkwise parallel algorithm gets messier, and you have to think carefully about numerical stability and about keeping the computation on tensor cores.

So if there's a contribution on my side, it's mostly at the foundation level. The chunkwise algorithms for the delta rule, the general framework of thinking about these models as online learning with different forgetting mechanisms, and the flash-linear-attention library, which a lot of people, including industry teams, use as a starting point for kernels and experiments. I was happy to see the ideas picked up and pushed further, and I had some discussions with people there. But I wouldn't want to overclaim. Taking a research idea and validating it at that scale is a different and very valuable kind of work, and the credit for that belongs to them.

To me, the more exciting part is what it signals for the field. Fine-grained decay plus the delta rule actually matters at scale, and linear attention hybrids are now serious candidates rather than just academic curiosities.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say my contribution was more conceptual than practical, honestly. The idea of fine-grained decay, decay that's per-channel or per-dimension rather than a single scalar per head or per token, isn't something I invented. It had been floating around for a while in different forms: Mamba's selective state space, GLA's data-dependent gating, even older RNN gating like LSTM forget gates are per-dimension. What I spent a lot of time on, with GLA and later with the flash-linear-attention library, was showing that you could actually make this efficient on hardware. People used to assume that if you made decay fine-grained, you'd lose the nice chunkwise parallel form and you'd be stuck with a slow recurrent scan. The chunkwise algorithms and the kernels in FLA were kind of a proof that no, you can have both.

So when Kimi was working on their linear attention design, I think the main thing they took from that line of work was that the engineering concern was already solved, which freed them to think about the modeling question. That's where I'd put my credit, if any: lowering the cost of trying these ideas, so that a team with real scale and real data could test what actually matters.

But I want to be careful here, because the hard part at Kimi's scale is not the kernel. It's the thousands of ablations, the hybrid layout decisions, how you combine it with full attention, the training stability at hundreds of billions of tokens. That's their work. I had some conversations with people there, and the open-source code was a starting point, but I wouldn't want to overstate it. I think the honest framing is: the research community, including me, built a set of tools and a set of hypotheses, and Kimi was one of the first to seriously validate them at frontier scale. That validation is in some ways more valuable than the original idea, because before that, a lot of people simply didn't believe linear attention with fine-grained gating would hold up.
